title: Case Study: Snake & Ladder
summary: A board of 100 cells, a dice, and two kinds of shortcuts. Design the classes behind Snake & Ladder and see why snakes and ladders are really the same class in disguise.

blocks.markdown:
Design **Snake & Ladder**: a board of 100 numbered cells, 2+ players taking turns, a **dice** that moves a player forward, **snakes** that drop you down, **ladders** that push you up. First player to land exactly on cell 100 wins.

- Sounds trivial to play, but it's a favorite LLD question — the payoff is spotting the **hidden symmetry** between snakes and ladders.
- Related: [case-study-tic-tac-toe](case-study-tic-tac-toe), [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework).

blocks.subTitle: Functional requirements
blocks.markdown:
What the system must support:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Board | Fixed size, 100 cells |
| Players | 2 or more, take turns |
| Movement | Dice roll advances current player |
| Shortcuts | Snake sends you down, ladder sends you up |
| Win | First to land exactly on the last cell |

Read the requirements as **nouns** (become classes) and **verbs** (become methods).

- **Board** — holds 100 cells and knows what's at each one.
- **Dice** — produces a random roll each turn.
- **Player** — has a name and a current position.
- **Snake / Ladder** — a start cell and an end cell that redirect a player.
- **Game** — owns the board, the players, and the turn loop.

The key insight: a **snake** and a **ladder** are structurally identical — both are "land on cell A, get **teleported** to cell B." Only the direction of B relative to A differs.

Model both as one class, **Jump** (`start`, `end`). The `Board` stores a single `map<cell, Jump>` instead of two separate collections — no `if isSnake / else isLadder` branching anywhere in the game logic.

Composition everywhere — no inheritance needed for this design.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Jump & Board
blocks.markdown:
```text
// A snake OR a ladder — same shape, opposite direction.
class Jump:
    start   // cell you land on to trigger it
    end     // cell you're moved to

    constructor(start, end):
        this.start = start
        this.end = end

class Board:
    size            // e.g. 100
    jumps           // map: cell -> Jump  (snakes AND ladders together)

    constructor(size, jumps):
        this.size = size
        this.jumps = jumps

    // returns the final cell after resolving any jump, or the same cell
    method resolve(cell):
        if this.jumps.has(cell):
            return this.jumps.get(cell).end
        return cell
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Dice & Player
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Dice:
    faces    // 6 for a standard die

    constructor(faces = 6):
        this.faces = faces

    method roll():
        return randomInt(1, this.faces)

class Player:
    name
    position    // current cell, starts at 0 (off-board)

    constructor(name):
        this.name = name
        this.position = 0
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: Game setup
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Game:
    board
    dice
    players    // queue — front of queue always plays next
    winner

    constructor(board, dice, playerNames):
        this.board = board
        this.dice = dice
        this.players = new Queue()
        for name in playerNames:
            this.players.enqueue(new Player(name))
        this.winner = null
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: the turn loop
blocks.markdown:
```text
method play():
    while this.winner == null:
        current = this.players.dequeue()
        this.playTurn(current)
        if current.position == this.board.size:
            this.winner = current
        else:
            this.players.enqueue(current)   // back of the line
    print(this.winner.name + " wins!")

method playTurn(player):
    roll = this.dice.roll()
    target = player.position + roll

    if target > this.board.size:
        return                              // overshoot — forfeit this turn

    player.position = this.board.resolve(target)
```

blocks.subTitle: Composition over inheritance
blocks.markdown:
It's tempting to make `Snake extends Jump` and `Ladder extends Jump`. Resist it — neither adds new fields or behavior, so subclassing buys nothing but two extra names.

One concrete `Jump(start, end)` used **compositionally** inside `Board` is simpler, and `resolve()` never needs to ask "which kind is this?" Whether a jump goes down (snake) or up (ladder) is just a fact about `start` vs `end`, not a separate type.

blocks.subTitle: Queue for turn order and Strategy for dice
blocks.markdown:
Two more small but interviewer-visible choices:

- **Queue of players** — turn order falls out naturally: dequeue, play, re-enqueue at the back. No manual index-tracking or modulo arithmetic.
- **Dice as its own class** (not an inline `random()` call) opens the door to the **Strategy pattern** — swap in a `WeightedDice` or `TwoDice` later without touching `Game`.

blocks.subTitle: Edge cases
blocks.markdown:
Cases that separate a working design from a half-baked one:

- **Overshoot** — a roll that would pass cell 100 must be ignored; the player stays put and the turn simply ends.
- **Chained jumps** — should landing at the end of a ladder ever chain into another jump? Standard rule: no, `resolve()` runs once per turn.
- **Multiple snakes/ladders on one cell** — invalid by construction if `jumps` is keyed by cell (a map can't hold two starts at once).

blocks.subTitle: Extensions
blocks.markdown:
The clean split makes extensions cheap:

- **Multiple dice** — `Dice.roll()` sums N dice; `Game` code doesn't change.
- **Rule variant: exact roll required, else skip** — already the default in `playTurn()`.
- **Bonus turn on rolling max face** — check the roll value in `playTurn()` and re-enqueue the same player at the front instead of the back.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling snakes and ladders uniformly
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you model snakes and ladders uniformly?**

Both are "land on cell A, teleport to cell B" — the only difference is whether B is below or above A, which is just data, not behavior. Model one `Jump(start, end)` class and store all snakes and ladders in the same `map<cell, Jump>` on the board. This kills any `isSnake/isLadder` branching in the game logic.

blocks.subTitle: How do you store the board
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you store the board and its jumps?**

The board itself just needs a `size` (100). Jumps go in a `map<cell, Jump>` keyed by the **start** cell — landing on a key means an instant lookup and redirect via `resolve(cell)`, instead of scanning a list of snakes and a list of ladders on every move.

blocks.subTitle: Handling overshoot
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you handle a dice roll that overshoots the last cell?**

Compute `target = position + roll` before touching state. If `target > boardSize`, the move is invalid — return early and skip the turn, leaving `position` unchanged. Only apply `board.resolve(target)` once the target is confirmed to be on the board.

blocks.subTitle: Supporting multiple dice
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you support rolling multiple dice at once?**

Keep `Dice` as its own class and give `Game` a list of dice (or a `diceCount`). `roll()` becomes the sum of each die's roll. Because `Game.playTurn()` only calls `dice.roll()` and never assumes a single six-sided die, this is a one-line change plus a constructor tweak — no ripple through the rest of the design.

blocks.subTitle: Why a queue for players
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why use a queue instead of an array with a turn index?**

A queue makes "whose turn is next" a structural fact instead of arithmetic — dequeue, play, enqueue at the back. It also makes special rules easy: skip a player by not re-enqueueing them, or grant a bonus turn by enqueueing at the front. An index-based array needs extra bookkeeping for the same cases.

blocks.subTitle: Extending to game variants
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you extend this design to a new variant, like a bonus turn on rolling a six?**

Check the roll's value inside `playTurn()` after calling `dice.roll()`, and conditionally enqueue the current player at the **front** of the queue instead of the back. `Board`, `Jump`, `Dice`, and `Player` stay untouched — the rule lives entirely in `Game`, which is exactly where a game-specific rule belongs.
